title: Candidate rejection feedback without legal risk: a recruiter's guide for Mac in 2026
metaTitle: Candidate rejection feedback without legal risk for recruiters
description: Write candidate rejection feedback that stays factual, job-related and consistent. Steps, costs, common mistakes and a week plan for recruiters using a Mac.

intro: To give candidate rejection feedback without legal risk, keep it short, factual and tied to the job criteria. Say the decision, name one job-related reason from a written requirement, and state the next step. This lowers your exposure. It does not remove it, so your employer's HR or legal team sets the final wording.
tldr: Say the decision, tie the reason to a written job requirement, and stop there.
Leave out guesses about personality, motives, age, health, family, or anything unrelated to the job.
Use one approved template per stage, and log what you sent and when.
Your employer's HR or legal team sets the rules. This page is practical guidance, not legal advice.

blocks.text: Most recruiters avoid writing rejection feedback for one reason. Any written reason can be read later, forwarded or quoted. So a one-line note with no reason feels like the safe choice. It often costs more than it saves, and the cost lands on your employer.
What candidate rejection feedback means in practice

Candidate rejection feedback is the message that tells an applicant a decision was made and, when it fits, why. It can be one sentence or a short paragraph. It can follow a CV screen, a phone call, a panel interview or a final round. The format changes with the stage. The rules for what you say do not change much.
What silence costs you

Silence has a cost, and it shows up later. A 2026 survey by Enhancv of 1,066 US job seekers found that 50.5% had been rejected at least once in the past year with no word from a human. Of those, 63.8% believed a machine made the decision. The survey came from a commercial publisher's panel, so treat it as a signal, not a census.

The cost to your employer brand is harder to measure, but the research leans one way. A 2004 meta-analysis of 86 independent samples, with a combined N of 48,750, linked positive applicant perceptions to recommending the employer and to intent to accept offers. Those links are correlational. They still point the same way as the rejection-letter study below.
The hiring cost behind every role

SHRM's benchmarking article, dated April 11, 2022, puts average cost per hire at nearly $4,700. The article does not name the survey, its year or its sample size, so use it as a rough anchor, not a precise budget. Edie Goldberg of E.L. Goldberg & Associates estimates total hiring cost at three to four times the position's salary. That is an expert estimate, not survey data.
A cold rejection also creates follow-up work. Here is what can happen next.

items: They ask for a reason in writing, and you spend time writing one from memory.
They share the experience with peers, which shapes how your employer is seen.
They decide not to apply again, so you lose a future applicant for a similar role.

blocks.text: Why recruiters skip feedback

The sources reviewed for this page do not explain the habit. So treat the causes below as working patterns, not findings from a study. They are common reasons, and you can test each one against your own inbox. Start with the ones that match your week.
What the rejection-letter research says about wording

A small study gives you some direction. It included 312 logistics applicants. Of those rejected at CV screening, 142 completed the survey, and 138 responses were analyzed. The team varied response time, formal or informal address, and personal or anonymous letters in a 2x2x2 design.

Shorter response time raised willingness to reapply, with 4.10 against 3.89. An informal address did the same, with 4.06 against 3.87. Response time, politeness and personalization had no main effect on perceived fairness. The sample is small, and some reported p-values need care. Treat these effects as suggestive, not settled.
Write feedback that stays inside the job

Feedback that carries legal risk usually does one of three things. It judges the person, guesses at motives, or talks about things the candidate cannot change that have nothing to do with the job. Keep each reason tied to a written requirement. The test is simple. Could you point to the job description and to evidence from the interview?

Compare two lines. The panel saw less launch planning experience than the role requires works. You seemed too quiet for this team does not. The second line judges a personality trait and says nothing about the job. It also invites an argument you cannot settle in an email.
A worked example for one rejected candidate

Say you are rejecting a candidate for a product marketing role after a panel interview. The job description asks for launch planning experience. The panel scored that area lower than the other finalists. Your message needs the stage, the decision, the requirement and a next step, and nothing more.

Here is a draft you can adapt. Thank you for interviewing with us for the Product Marketing Manager role. We will not be moving forward. The panel felt another candidate had more hands-on launch planning experience, which the role requires. If a role closer to your launch work opens, we would welcome a new application. Best wishes with your search.

blocks.title: Check before you send
blocks.text: Read the draft once as the candidate would. If a line mentions age, health, family, or how someone seems, delete it. Then ask HR or legal about anything you are still unsure of.
Common mistakes that create the most risk

items: Naming a reason you cannot tie to a written requirement.
Copying an old template that nobody has checked since it was written.
Writing the feedback from memory weeks after the interview.
Sending from a personal account with no copy kept anywhere.
Adding a new reason when a candidate pushes back on the phone.
Sending a rejection before the hiring decision is final, which causes confusion.

blocks.text: Set up one template per stage on your Mac

A Mac mail app will not stop you from typing the same message again and again. Apple Mail has no built-in template feature, according to a blog from a mail app maker. Apple's own Mail guide describes reply suggestions from Apple Intelligence, but it does not mention saved templates. Check the behavior on your own Mac before you rely on it.
Templates mailbox workaround in Apple Mail

One workaround uses a Templates mailbox. Choose Mailbox > New Mailbox and name it Templates. Write the message, leave the To field empty, and save it in that mailbox. When you need it, reopen the saved message through Message > Send Again. Fill in the candidate's name and the role, then review the whole message before you send.
Text Replacements for the lines you reuse

Text Replacements work well for short closing lines. Go to System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements. Add a replacement with a short trigger you would never type by accident, and paste the full line as the replacement. Apple's support page says selected replacements can be dragged to the desktop as a backup file.

If iCloud Drive is on for each device, and the same Apple Account is signed in, replacements can sync across Apple devices. Sync is optional. Signatures under Mail > Settings > Signatures suit closing blocks only. Keep the body of each rejection in a template, not in a signature.
Keep a record in Gmail and Google Sheets

A rejection message is half the job. The other half is a record of what you said, which criteria you used and when you sent it. Keep one row per candidate in [Google Sheets for recruiters](/for/recruiters/google-sheets). Useful columns include role, stage, decision date, requirement missed, template version and sender.

Gmail can help with timing. Scheduled send lets you queue a batch of feedback for a set time, so the messages go out together. The steps are on our [Gmail for recruiters](/for/recruiters/gmail) page. Keep each batch small enough that you can still check every message.
When to stop and ask HR or legal

Some cases need a person before a word goes out. Stop and ask HR or legal if a candidate asks for specific reasons in writing, names a complaint, mentions a disability or leave, or says the decision was unfair. Ask the same if you are unsure which local hiring rules apply.

If you recruit for regulated roles, such as nursing, law or accounting, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data. Do not paste candidate records or client details into a tool unless your employer's policy allows it. When in doubt, keep the details out of the message.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It can point at things, guide you one click at a time, and draft or type text. Lazur does not send your email, click buttons or operate other apps for you.

Dictation fits the criteria notes. Hold fn and speak the requirement, the evidence and the decision in plain words. Then edit the result before it reaches a candidate. Lazur also keeps snippets, a personal dictionary and clipboard slots for the closing lines you reuse.
After you send

Log the send the same day. If the candidate replies, answer only from the record you made at the time. Pass questions about rights, complaints or legal steps to HR or legal before you reply. Review your templates on a fixed schedule, so old wording does not stay in circulation.

The best feedback process is dull. It uses the same sheet, the same three-part message and the same review step every time. Dull is easier to explain later, and easier to defend when someone asks what happened.

faq.question: Does a rejection email have to give a reason?
faq.answer: No single rule applies everywhere. Many employers choose a short, job-related reason, because it reads as fair. Ask your HR or legal team what your employer requires for each stage and each location.

faq.question: Can I get candidate rejection feedback without legal risk at all?
faq.answer: You can lower the risk, but you cannot remove it. Keep feedback factual, job-related and consistent, and have HR or legal approve the wording. This page is practical guidance, not legal advice.

faq.question: What should I never write in rejection feedback?
faq.answer: Avoid comments on personal traits, guesses about motives, and anything unrelated to the job, including personal life. If you are not sure a comment is safe, leave it out and check with HR.

faq.question: Can I use an AI tool to draft rejection messages?
faq.answer: Check your employer's policy first. Do not paste candidate records or personal details into any tool unless your employer allows it. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored.

faq.question: Does Apple Mail have templates?
faq.answer: Not in the way many people expect, according to a blog from a mail app maker. The Templates mailbox workaround and Text Replacements are common alternatives. Apple's Mail guide describes reply suggestions but does not mention saved templates.

faq.question: How soon should I send rejection feedback?
faq.answer: In a small study, shorter response time raised willingness to reapply, with 4.10 against 3.89. Pick a fixed window after each decision, and let your team agree on it. Speed helps, but accuracy matters more.

faq.question: What if a candidate asks for a full written explanation?
faq.answer: Do not write a new explanation from memory. Use the criteria sheet and the notes you made at the time. If the request goes further, such as a complaint or a claim, pass it to HR or legal.

faq.question: Should the tone of rejection feedback be informal?
faq.answer: Not always. An informal letter raised reapply intent in a small study, with 4.06 against 3.87. Match the tone your employer already uses with candidates, and keep it consistent across roles.

faq.question: How strong is the research on rejection letters?
faq.answer: It is suggestive, not settled. The rejection-letter study analyzed 138 responses, and its links are correlational. The 2004 meta-analysis is broader, with 86 samples, but it covers applicant perceptions in general.

costs.title: Silence costs you a future applicant
costs.text: A rejection with no reason can make a candidate less likely to come back. In a small study, perceived fairness predicted willingness to reapply, with β=0.667. The link is correlational, so treat it as a warning sign, not proof.

costs.title: Your employer brand takes the hit
costs.text: Candidates talk to peers and form views about your company. In the same small study, perceived fairness predicted recommending the employer, with β=0.745. Cold, unexplained rejections make that harder to earn back.

costs.title: Every open role already costs money
costs.text: SHRM puts average cost per hire at nearly $4,700 in its 2022 benchmarking article. An expert estimate from Edie Goldberg puts total hiring cost at three to four times the salary. Feedback is a small slice of that spend, but a long, messy hire costs more.

costs.title: Rework lands on your desk
costs.text: Each candidate who writes back with questions creates more work. You may answer, forward the question to HR, or explain your reasoning again. None of that time shows up in the template you sent. Log the follow-ups for one month to see the real load.

costs.title: Legal exposure you cannot price
costs.text: A vague note is not automatically a problem. A message that cites a personal trait, guesses at motives or mentions unrelated facts can start a dispute. The sources for this page have no figure for what that costs. Ask HR or legal what a dispute would cost your employer.

causes.title: Fear of legal exposure
causes.text: A common reaction is to say nothing, because a written reason can be quoted later. The fear is understandable. A one-line note feels safer than a reason. But silence also removes the record of a fair, job-related decision, which is the evidence you need.

causes.title: Too many candidates, too little time
causes.text: Volume is a common reason. One open role can bring in many applications, and each one needs a decision. Writing a specific reason for each takes time nobody budgets for. The sources reviewed here have no figure for recruiter workload, so treat this as a pattern.

causes.title: No written criteria
causes.text: If the requirements live in your head or in a chat thread, you cannot write a reason that fits. The reason then sounds vague or made up. Write the core requirements before the first interview, and share them with the panel so everyone uses the same words.

causes.title: Nobody owns the message
causes.text: Recruiters, hiring managers and HR can each assume someone else sends the note. The candidate waits, and the message never goes out. Name one owner per role at the start. Write that person's name into the tracker next to each candidate.

causes.title: Old templates with old wording
causes.text: Templates get copied from one role to the next. They carry phrases nobody checked, including remarks about age, health or personal life. A line that read fine last year can read badly now. Review each shared template with HR or legal at least once.

causes.title: Screening that no human sees
causes.text: Some applicants are screened out before a person reads the CV. The 2026 survey found that 63.8% of those rejected without human contact believed a machine made the decision. Know how your screening works, so you can describe it accurately if a candidate asks.

fixes.title: Write the criteria before you read CVs
fixes.text: Keep a one-page sheet for each role. List the requirements, the evidence you expect and the stage where each one is judged. When you reject someone, the reason is already on the page. Google Sheets in Chrome works well for this, with one tab per role.

fixes.title: Use the same three parts every time
fixes.text: Every rejection can use three parts. State the decision, give one job-related reason, and name the next step if there is one. Keep the parts in the same order. Consistency makes the message easier to check and easier to defend.

fixes.title: Send sooner, in a batch
fixes.text: The rejection-letter study found that shorter response time raised willingness to reapply, with 4.10 against 3.89. Pick a fixed window for feedback after each decision. Gmail scheduled send can queue a batch for a set time, so the messages go out together.

fixes.title: Match the tone your employer uses
fixes.text: In the same study, an informal address raised reapply intent, with 4.06 against 3.87. That fits some companies. It may not suit a formal client or a regulated business. Use the voice your employer already uses with candidates, and do not borrow a tone you cannot support.

fixes.title: Build templates on your Mac
fixes.text: Set up a Templates mailbox in Apple Mail for full messages. Use Text Replacements under System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements for short closing lines. Test each template on your own address before you use it with a candidate.

fixes.title: Get one HR or legal review
fixes.text: Ask HR or legal to approve each template once for each stage. Keep the approved version in one place, with the approval date at the top. That way you know which wording each candidate received, and you can prove it later.

fixes.title: Keep a send log
fixes.text: Record each rejection with the date, the role, the stage, the template version and the sender. The log is your proof of what was said and when. Keep only the details you need, and leave out sensitive personal information.

fixes.title: Answer follow-ups from the record
fixes.text: If a candidate asks for more detail, answer from the criteria sheet and your notes from the time. Do not invent a new reason on the spot. If the question is about a legal right or a complaint, pass it to HR or legal before you reply.

fixes.title: Batch the work once a week
fixes.text: Send feedback in one block each week, rather than as each interview ends. A batch keeps the wording consistent and cuts the number of times you switch tasks. Set a recurring reminder in Apple Reminders for the same slot each week.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Write the criteria sheet
plan.text: Pick one open role. List its requirements and the stage where each one is judged. Save the sheet in Google Sheets in Chrome, with one tab for that role.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Draft one template per stage
plan.text: Write a template for the CV screen, the phone screen and the final interview. Keep each one to a short decision, one job-related reason and a next step.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Get HR or legal review
plan.text: Send the templates to HR or legal. Ask them to flag any wording that refers to personal traits, motives or unrelated facts. Save the approved version with the approval date.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Set up your Mac shortcuts
plan.text: Create the Templates mailbox in Apple Mail, and add Text Replacements for short closing lines. Send one test message to yourself before you use the setup with a candidate.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Send and log in one batch
plan.text: Send this week's feedback in one block. Use Gmail scheduled send if you want the batch to go out at a set time. Log each send with the date and the template version.

plan.label: Next week
plan.title: Review the log
plan.text: Look for patterns in the log. Check for follow-up questions that came back, stages with no reason on file, and any template that needs a rewrite before the next round.
